cards.front: When you turn left from a one-way road onto a two-way road, which lane do you turn into?
cards.back: When you turn left from a one-way road onto a two-way road, turn into the lane just to the right of the center line.

cards.front: After that turn, what must you do before moving to the right lane?
cards.back: After that turn, check traffic on your right and signal a lane change before you move over to the right lane.

cards.front: May a left turn from a one-way road onto a two-way road be made against a red light?
cards.back: A left turn from a one-way road onto a two-way road can never be made against a red light.

cards.front: Where does the one-way to two-way left turn end, and may it be made on red?
cards.back: The left turn from a one-way road onto a two-way road ends in the lane just right of the center line and may not be made on a red light.

decks.domain: The one-way to two-way left turn, two-way left turn lanes, and METRO light rail safety for drivers, bike riders, walkers and children

cards.front: What is the middle lane on many two-way streets painted as?
cards.back: On many two-way streets, the middle lane is painted as a shared left turn lane for both directions.

cards.front: How is a two-way left turn lane edged?
cards.back: A two-way left turn lane is edged on each side by a pair of yellow lines, with the inner line broken and the outer line solid.

cards.front: Which line of a two-way left turn lane is broken, and which is solid?
cards.back: Along a two-way left turn lane the broken yellow line is the inner line next to the center lane, while the solid yellow line is the outer line.

cards.front: Who may use a two-way left turn lane?
cards.back: A two-way left turn lane may be used only by vehicles turning left, from either direction.

cards.front: What two uses does the two-way left turn lane allow?
cards.back: The two-way left turn lane gives you a safe place to slow down before turning left off the street, or to pull into when turning left out of a side street or driveway.

cards.front: May you use the two-way left turn lane to pull out of a driveway or to speed up and merge?
cards.back: You may pull into the two-way left turn lane when turning left out of a driveway, but you may not use it to speed up and merge with through traffic.

cards.front: May you slow down in the two-way left turn lane, and may you pass in it?
cards.back: Slowing in the two-way left turn lane before a left turn is allowed, while passing or driving straight through in it is not.

cards.front: What should you do before entering a two-way left turn lane?
cards.back: Signal before you enter a two-way left turn lane.

cards.front: How far should your vehicle move into the two-way left turn lane?
cards.back: Move your vehicle completely into the two-way left turn lane.

cards.front: Whom should you watch for in a two-way left turn lane?
cards.back: Watch for other drivers who are also using the two-way left turn lane.

cards.front: What must you never use the two-way left turn lane for?
cards.back: Never use the two-way left turn lane to pass, to travel straight through, or to speed up so you can merge with through traffic.

cards.front: Where do METRO light rail trains run, and how does car traffic relate to them?
cards.back: METRO light rail trains run on streets in the Valley in Maricopa County, and car traffic moves right alongside them.

cards.front: What pedestrian safety work was done along the METRO line?
cards.back: Pedestrian safety work along the METRO line includes countdown signals, new walkways and landscaping meant to cut down on jaywalking.

cards.front: What did some crossings near schools receive in the METRO design?
cards.back: Some crossings near schools received new signals as part of the METRO safety design.

cards.front: From where may a car turn across the METRO tracks?
cards.back: A car may turn across the METRO tracks only from a designated turn lane that has its own traffic signal control.

cards.front: How is the METRO trackway set apart from traffic?
cards.back: METRO trains travel in their own trackway, set apart from traffic by six-inch curbs.

cards.front: Where may cars cross the METRO trackway?
cards.back: Cars may cross the METRO trackway only at controlled locations, where special signals and warning signs switch on as a train approaches.

cards.front: How do turning across the tracks and crossing the trackway differ?
cards.back: Turning across the METRO tracks is allowed only from signal-controlled turn lanes, and crossing the trackway is allowed only at controlled locations.

cards.front: How are METRO station access points reached?
cards.back: Each METRO station has two access points, and both are reached by a signalized crosswalk.

cards.front: Why can riders board METRO trains without a step?
cards.back: METRO station platforms sit at the same height as the train floor, so riders board without a step.

cards.front: How are frontage roads near the METRO tracks controlled?
cards.back: Frontage roads near the METRO tracks are controlled by traffic signals and built to handle large trucks and emergency vehicles.

cards.front: When can a METRO train move?
cards.back: A METRO train cannot move until its doors have closed.

cards.front: How are light rail couplers made safer in a crash?
cards.back: The couplers that join light rail vehicles are covered in an energy-absorbing material to reduce injuries in a crash.

decks.domain: The one-way to two-way left turn, two-way left turn lanes, and METRO light rail safety for drivers, bike riders, walkers and children

cards.front: What do electronic Train Approaching signs do?
cards.back: Electronic Train Approaching signs at every METRO light rail intersection flash when a train is coming toward the intersection.

cards.front: Why are U-turns allowed at almost every light rail intersection?
cards.back: U-turns are allowed at almost every light rail intersection along the twenty-mile METRO system so that vehicles can cross the tracks.

cards.front: How are left turns and U-turns controlled at light rail intersections?
cards.back: At light rail intersections, left turns and U-turns are controlled by traffic signals.

cards.front: How does the Train Approaching sign differ from the combined U-turn and left turn sign?
cards.back: A flashing Train Approaching sign warns that a train is coming, while the combined U-turn and left turn sign marks the signal-controlled turns used to cross the tracks.

cards.front: Where must you never stop or park a car or bike?
cards.back: Never stop or park a car or a bike on light rail tracks.

cards.front: At a light rail crossing, what do a red signal and a red arrow mean?
cards.back: At light rail crossings, stop on a red signal, and treat a red arrow as an order not to turn.

cards.front: What is the difference between a red signal and a red arrow at a light rail crossing?
cards.back: A red signal at a light rail crossing means stop, and a red arrow means do not turn.

cards.front: What should you do before crossing light rail tracks by car or bike?
cards.back: Look both ways before you cross the light rail tracks, whether you are driving or biking.

cards.front: Where must you never drive a car or ride a bike?
cards.back: Never drive a car or ride a bike in the lane where the train operates.
cards.memory_hook: stay out of the train lane

cards.front: Why should you watch and listen carefully near the tracks?
cards.back: Light rail trains make little noise, so near the tracks watch for their flashing headlights and listen for their bells and horns.

cards.front: Can you rely on hearing a light rail train?
cards.back: A quiet train means you cannot rely on hearing it, so you look for flashing headlights and also listen for its bells and horns.

cards.front: How can you tell whether a light rail train is coming toward you or moving away?
cards.back: Both ends of a light rail train look alike, so white headlights mean it is coming toward you and red taillights mean it is moving away.

cards.front: What do white headlights and red taillights on a light rail train tell you?
cards.back: White headlights mean a light rail train is approaching, while red taillights mean it is moving away from you.

decks.module: Walking and children near light rail
decks.domain: The one-way to two-way left turn, two-way left turn lanes, and METRO light rail safety for drivers, bike riders, walkers and children

cards.front: Where should pedestrians not walk or stand near light rail?
cards.back: Pedestrians should not walk on the light rail tracks or stand close to them.

cards.front: Where should pedestrians cross near light rail?
cards.back: Pedestrians near light rail should cross only at crosswalks and follow the crosswalk signals.

cards.front: What track rules apply to drivers and to pedestrians?
cards.back: Drivers must never stop or park on the tracks, and pedestrians must never walk on them or stand close to them.

cards.front: What should adults do with small children near the tracks and on platforms?
cards.back: Adults should hold small children by the hand near the tracks and on station platforms.

cards.front: What should children do around light rail tracks?
cards.back: Children should stop, look and listen whenever they are around light rail tracks.

cards.front: What should children do with bikes and skateboards at crosswalks near light rail?
cards.back: At crosswalks near light rail, children should get off their bikes and skateboards and walk them across.

cards.front: What do children do with bikes and skateboards at a light rail crosswalk?
cards.back: At a light rail crosswalk, children walk their bikes and skateboards across instead of riding them.

cards.front: Where should children never play?
cards.back: Children should never play near the light rail tracks.

recap_hooks.text: From a one-way road onto a two-way road, end just right of the center line, signal before moving right, and never make the turn on red.
The shared center lane is for left turns only: signal, move fully in, and never use it to pass, drive through or merge.
Turn across the METRO tracks only from signal-controlled lanes, and cross the trackway only at controlled locations.
Never stop on the tracks or drive in the train lane, stop on red, treat a red arrow as no turn, and read white headlights as coming.

recaps.module: Walking and children near light rail

recap_hooks.text: Pedestrians stay off the tracks and use crosswalks, adults hold small children's hands, and children walk their wheels across.
